thread.title: Apple: Continue To Expect Earnings Risk - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Elazar Advisors, LLC
title: Apple: Continue To Expect Earnings Risk - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Here's what we concluded on Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) just a week a go, Dec. 26 ,
"There's no argument that Apple is a great company. However, as we warned in November, growth rates have been slowing down. We'd expect there are continued headwinds that can continue that slowing trend. That slowing trend can drive earnings risk which would mean stock risk when they report in late January/early February."
Apple Didn't Account For China In Their Last Earnings Guidance We lined up three main downside drivers at the time - emerging markets, the dollar and China.
With China, the company had not seen weakness as of their prior earnings call, so China risk was not reflected in their guidance for this quarter.
Here's what we said last week,
"What concerns us is that China was not mentioned as a soft spot in their weak guidance last quarter.
Given the macro slowdown in China I would guess that's another shoe to drop come this or next quarter. It could be the newest reason for a continued slower revenue growth trend in the coming quarters."
Here's what Apple just said ,
"While we anticipated some challenges in key emerging markets, we did not foresee the magnitude of the economic deceleration, particularly in Greater China. In fact, most of our revenue shortfall to our guidance, and over 100 percent of our year-over-year worldwide revenue decline, occurred in Greater China across iPhone, Mac and iPad."
China was in fact the next shoe to drop as we were concerned about and warned you last week and in November.
Where Are Numbers Going? Earnings drive stocks. Let's see where numbers are going.
Apple's new revenue guidance is for $84B, or -4.9% year-over-year. That is a massive slowdown from the September quarter's growth rate of 19.6%.
When Apple last reported everybody thought the company's 3% revenue growth guide for the December quarter was way too conservative. We didn't.
After their last earnings in November we wrote ,
"So, really a 1.6% slowdown from September to December over a couple of years smoothing out channel fill timing does not seem too conservative.
Conclusion: Not conservative."
Let's review what that means and update where revenues can now go in 2019 based on their new guidance.
The company complained about a shift in timing of new products but we smoothed all that out looking at multi-year revenue growth trends.
If you look at one year growth rates, yes, timing can throw off the numbers. But when you use two- and three-year revenue growth trends it smoothes out one-time factors like these timing shifts.
In our November report we averaged the two-year revenue growth for this year and last year. For September that came out to 17.5%. The December guide they gave back in November implied an average two-year growth rate of 15.9%.
So they didn't really expect much of a slowdown in that December guide when factoring in tougher year-ago compares.
The two-year comparison from last year was 13% more difficult in December vs. September. Many people ignore these critical facts. Their guide assumed a 16.5% slowdown. But taking the year-ago tougher comparison into account they were only looking for a 3.5% multi-year slowdown in December which was not super conservative.
Let's Review The New Guide: There's More Earnings Risk

The new guide for the December quarter is $84B. That assumes a -4.9% revenue growth rate. But look at the two-year. That's what matters. That's a massive slowdown from 31.9% to 7.8%. Wow, right? Oh my that's a big slowdown.
I have to model a continued two-year slowdown, but I'm being way too nice. A drop from 31.9% to 7.8% this quarter is a 24% drop. March can continue to drop big but I'm only using a 1% 2-year slowdown from December but it probably needs to be worse.
Still, not reflecting the full potential drop for the March quarter we get $55B in revenues for the March quarter vs. the Street's $64B. Ouch.
That should come down but could you imagine if they guide in late January $9B below the Street? Ouch. That won't be good.
For the year as a whole, add it up, we get $239B, but the Street's currently at $278B. We are about $40B below the Street for fiscal 2019. The Street is not factoring in any slowdown in the two-year or the tougher year-ago numbers.
The Street tends to ignore the two-year trends. We don't. We find that companies guidance ends up aligning with two-year trends.
Our EPS end up being $10.47 (Full model: pay wall) for the coming fiscal year vs. the Street's $13.29. They'll bring that down.
Great Company, But Can't Ignore The Earnings Trends As you know we say we don't fall in love with companies we fall in love with earnings. Companies can be great companies but you have to respect the earnings. Stocks are valued based on earnings.
I don't want to get sold on stories or general phrases like "great company." I think that's a mistake unless you can put it away for five years and not look at it and not sell at the bottom when it gets too bad.
I'm focused on the next 1-2 quarters as our guide to determine our next year's earnings numbers. That EPS is what should drive the stock price.
Companies look out one year and very much respect investors that have that time horizon. It's not too short term. That's the time horizon that I believe drives stocks.
For Apple we have continued EPS downside risk so holding the shares continues to be a risk as we've been warning.
Conclusion Apple had a bombshell today for markets. I don't think our readers and subscribers were so shocked. If you did the math and thought about China slowing, it was tough for Apple to dodge the slowdown.
We've been saying to subscribers and publicly that Q3 was weak for tech, Q4 is likely worse and Q1's guides should be even worse. Apple is early confirmation of that.
Be careful this earnings season.
